HIGH WATER LEVEL IN LAKE ONTARIO-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under Standing Order 43 to propose a motion on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. In view of the increasingly serious threat posed by high water levels on the Great Lakes, a problem now emphasized by the evacuation of more families from their homes along Lake Ontario, I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Beattie):
That the government immediately take emergency measures to relieve the hardship suffered by residents of East Hamilton, Salt-fleet Township and other areas, who have been flooded out of their homes along the shores of Lake Ontario, and that the government take short and long-term measures to avoid further threats to the well-being and property of those families.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 43,1 request the unanimous consent of the House to move a motion related to a very important matter which is undoubtedly pressing.
It has to do with workers who are screened by manpower centres for retraining in their trade in order to meet the requirements of demand on labour market as well as trade and work regulations and who lose their entitlement to extra unemployment insurance benefits for the duration of this training. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Charlevoix (Mr. Caouette):
That a special House of Commons committee be instructed to study this serious problem and to make relevant recommendations for amendments to the act and the regulations as well as to Department of Manpower programs tending to facilitate better co-operation between manpower centres and unemployment insurance offices.

speechtext:
1.	Is any branch or division of the Department of National Health and Welfare pursuing any program of research into the feasibility of the possible practice of acupuncture in Canada and, if so, what is the nature and extent of research and how many researchers are involved?
2.	How many individuals or groups have suggested the clinical utilization of acupuncture techniques?
3.	Has the Department positive knowledge of acupuncture technique being used in Canada and, if so, what and how frequently?

May 23, 1973
Order Paper Questions

Mr. Speaker, in the few minutes allowed me, I would like to express my views on the important question of the abolition of the death penalty or the retention of certain restrictions in the act, restrictions which have been incorporated since 1967 in the Criminal Code, as stipulated by Bill C-2 now before the House, with a view to extending those restrictions for another five years.
Mr. Speaker many hon. members have already spoken on this subject, and I must say I followed the debate very closely in order to weigh the pros and cons of that important matter, in the light of the research I have done, just as the other hon. members did, I am sure.
Unfortunately, I am disappointed with the way this debate is shaping out; once again we find that statistics are tricky to manipulate and that, on occasion, they can be misleading.
I see that hon. members in favour of passing this bill currently before us enlighten their speeches with official statistics showing that the existence of capital punishment has no effect in Canada or in other countries that they mentioned in their remarks.
On the other hand, those among us who want capital punishment in Canada to become really effective, as prior to 1967, are trying to prove with official statistics that since capital punishment was abolished the rate of major *
Capital Punishment
crimes has increased in Canada, precisely as a result of that abolition.
I think that in fact capital punishment still exists in Canada. Thugs and professional killers and all the others who continue as I speak to take it upon themselves to inflict capital punishment but through illegality and crime-call it assassination or whatever you want-kill shamelessly and without any fear of justice those who stand in their way. They mercilessly riddle with bullets all those who could prevent them from committing their rapes, robberies or other crimes. I think that they are now the unchallenged masters in Canada because they no longer fear the gallows, and I think that fear is the beginning of wisdom. They are increasingly becoming masters everywhere.
That is why I blame this government for not administering the act as passed in 1967. There have been many murders of policemen and prison guards since 1967, and all criminals convicted of those reprehensible acts were reprieved in last recourse by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) or the Governor in Council.
I do not wish to produce here tons of statistics to show whether capital punishment influences criminals or not. Moreover, I have dealt with the matter on several occasions in this House during the last parliament and I then quoted statistics in support of my speech.
Today, I wish to make my position clear and according to my conscience, I should take a logical and reasonable stand. I had then consistently asked for restoration of the death penalty and I have not changed my mind.
I think that my role is to state in the House what are my constituents' views as if they were present.
Mr. Speaker, I have promised my constituents after my first election to seek their advice on every important matter of general interest concerning the Criminal Code or any other legislation coming under federal jurisdiction.
I have therefore held information meetings in the past- I still do-and taken the habit of contacting my electors at least every month on any subject of concern which is bound to have an effect on their life. In the light of their answers, I can make up my mind more easily and truly say what they think on the basis of papers in my possession.
So, during the last election campaign, I confirmed to my electors that I would uphold my position on this matter and they approved me. And I think that they approve my habit of consulting them, because I was elected with a stronger majority than in 1968. In October 1971, I asked all voters of the Richmond riding to express themselves on the restoration of the death penalty and more than 25 per cent answered my questionnaire. Of these 25 per cent, 92.6 per cent were in favour of restoring capital punishment as it existed in 1967. And I sincerely believe that at this time the percentage of those in favour of reinstating capital punishment in Canada would be still higher.
Mr. Speaker, my decision has therefore been taken in the light of the wishes expressed by my constituents, and I insist on pointing out to the House that I shall vote against Bill C-2 tending to suspend capital punishment in certain cases. I am in favour of the reinstatement of capital pun-

Capital Punishment
ishment in all cases where the guilt of the accused has been established without any doubt whoever his victim might be. I shall even go so far as to extend application of this punishment to abortionists who bring death to children who have the right to life.
In order to justify their wish to vote in favour of this legislation, a number of people will resort to such arguments as dignity, the right to life for murderers, and moral progress. I wish to point out incidentally that I differ from the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Macln-nis) who, a few days ago, urged the government to eliminate capital punishment from the Criminal Code, whereas for the past five years she has repeatedly been asking the government to legalize abortion in Canada.
In my opinion, an individual who deliberately provokes an abortion should, after adequate evidence, be punishable by death and such a provision should be introduced into the Criminal Code.
Mr. Speaker, those who want to abolish capital punishment from the Criminal Code resort to weak and contradictory arguments. Have they considered for a single moment that it is society's strict obligation to protect the integrity of the individual against all that threatens it? I suggest that murderers are a threat, directly or indirectly, to society.
In my opinion, the legislator born of a society which has elected to be respected and respectable must punish the individual who is really found guilty of having willfully taken the life of one of his fellow citizens. Moreover, the Canadian legislator who, owing to his duties, is responsible for protecting the members of that society, must give the courts, by including some provisions in the Criminal Code, the necessary tools in order that the chief justice of the court and the jury might, if they wish, prescribe capital punishment for the individual guilty of the premeditated murder of a policeman or anybody else.
I have already said and I repeat that, at birth, the individual is pacific and that it is our society which makes him aggressive, nervous and unsociable. One of the reasons for this is the apathy shown by the parents in assuming their responsibilities towards their children, for too many young mothers work outside home to make both ends meet or pay the income tax. A child left to himself, without his mother and often without supervision, starts to commit minor offences against the society around him and sometimes against himself, and as he grows these offences grow correspondingly bigger.
Our modern society also contains the monstrosities that are called "schools" or "colleges", in which, supposedly to increase efficiency, 1,500, 2,000 or even 3,000 pupils are heaped together, almost without supervision because there are too many of them; these school children, who are often quite young-from 9 to 15 years old-are treated like numbers. I call these groups of schoolchildren school herds, in which the child is deprived of the love and understanding of his teacher, society and those around him.
Our governments have failed, in my opinion, to get to the roots of crimes committed by groups of young people. Every day one sees young children, in school or elsewhere,

committing offences, using drugs, etc. for lack of supervision.
I admit, Mr. Speaker, that this is a large-scale undertaking that would require a lot of patience and effort, but I am convinced that the only way to abolish the death penalty, which is the matter before us, would be to take better care of society before young people, especially, start to commit offences. Our schools should become more humane, while aiming also at providing education and instruction. At present, we hand out instruction to students, but when they leave school with their diplomas, there is no place for them in our society. That is why we see so many young people aged between 17 and 25 turning to crime.
Young people, Mr. Speaker, are our future. It is incumbent upon us to give our young people everything they need to succeed in life. Thus we would see no more unbalanced people steal and sometimes, under too strong a tension or from the effect of drugs, kill to get what they want.
Let us give young couples the possibility of raising their children in happiness and safety without their having to wonder always about their future. Let us legislate so that we can live under a system of distributive justice, of comprehension and love where money, luxury as we know it, vanity and envy are no longer the masters of our destinies and then we will not longer be required to discuss a bill such as the one before us now.
Finally, I rhust say that we should rid Canadian society of its undesirable citizens but even more I think that the government should seriously consider the deep-rooted reasons which prompt society to adopt such a legislation. In my opinion, I think members of Parliament and the federal and provincial governments, because they have adopted certain laws, are mainly responsible for this high proportion of murderers. A murderer is an individual who spent his childhood in the street. He has grown up like a tree; in my opinion, we surely should grant more importance to the surveillance of young people in our society. Thus, tomorrow we will be able to see a responsible and flourishing society flourish and people who will learn to enjoy life.

subsubtopic: REINSTATEMENT OF LAW RELATING TO CAPITAL PUNISHMENT THAT EXISTED PRIOR TO DECEMBER 30, 1972
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to place on the record, as have many members, my views on this bill and on the matter of capital punishment. Perhaps this is one of the most important problems with which this parliament will have to contend. The end result will likely be very little different from that of the present situation. It is good the House will have a free vote on this matter. I think the discussion will be useful to whatever will be the ultimate decision.
It is significant that in western civilization the death penalty at least has been steadily eliminated and is now applied only to so-called capital murder. Since legislation on this matter was last passed in this House no death sentences have been carried out on persons convicted of killing prison guards or policemen; these cases have all been commuted by the Governor General on orders from the cabinet.
May 23, 1973

There has been widespread discussion on whether capital punishment acts as a deterrent to those who would commit murder. From my observation of murder cases about which I have personal knowledge, the deterrence of capital punishment was only vaguely recognized by the murderer when he carried out his crime. My position with regard to capital punishment being a deterrent to an individual carrying out the act of murder is that it is very secondary.
Man is essentially a creature that is both aggressive and suspicious. Wars and acts of violence seem to be a legacy in our long history of evolution and development. By nature, man is a violent person at times. The overlay of social conscience, customs and inhibitions seems to have determined that society will obey considerable restrictions in order that people may live in communities and obey some laws. It is interesting to note that when our cities become increasingly congested, there are increasing acts of violence, murder and rape. The people in these large cities become depersonalized and have little interest in what is happening to individuals about them.
My own feeling is that most murderers are of distinct personality types. Whether or not they are insane, as has been assumed in many successful defences of murder cases, I think it can be said that certain mental states will cause temporary loss of normal inhibitions and murder may take place. It has been insufficiently recognized that a murderer is a distinct personality type and commits murder according to his own dictates and ideas. Also, it has not been recognized that these people always will have such personality deficiencies. Faced with the same circumstances, a murderer will always repeat the crime. To him, that is the immediate solution to the problem and he can see no other way. With this in mind, I believe these people must be removed from society. There are two obvious ways in which this can be done. The first is the institution of capital punishment whereby the murderer is put to death. The state is thus spared much expense and society is protected from the murderer forever.
I am reminded of an answer to a questionnaire sent out by a member of this House. The respondent's reply was: "I am for capital punishment. It may not be a deterrent, but at least it prevents repetition." The second solution would be to lock up the murderer for the rest of his natural life. In this way society would be protected from individuals who had committed murder. It would be simple to assume that the first solution, the removal of the murderer from society by death, would be easy, final and would recommend itself to many people. However, I believe that this final solution does not remove the risk of putting to death those who are innocent but happened to be in a circumstantial position whereby suspicion was laid upon them.
After an innocent person is condemned to death and suffers the ultimate fate, society in no way can repay him for the loss of his life. But if he is confined to prison by misadventure and is serving a sentence, society can make some recompense to him for the injustice and punishment that has been meted out to him.
My position on capital punishment is that if I were sure that justice was always right and that the accused had
Capital Punishment
committed a crime, I would not hesitate to have the death penalty carried out. But history is full of significant miscarriages of justice, and at times innocent people have suffered the death penalty.
In times of great national emergency this might well be a necessity and people might find themselves unfairly but inadvertently victimized. In the normal course of events, which regard to murder that occurs in society we should take all precautions possible to make sure that the innocent are not convicted and lose their lives. In other words, I feel that the risk of making an error is greater than the value obtained from the deterrent effect of capital punishment.
At this time there have been no convincing figures to show that capital punishment acts as a deterrent, at least in what is called normal times in our society. Perhaps at some time in the future we will have to recognize this or that statistic, and other indices may show that capital punishment is necessary as a deterrent. But that time is not yet, and I do not think this House has to vote for capital punishment on the basis that only in this way will murders be reduced, or because the incidence of murder is getting out of hand.
I stated previously that murderers had a definite personality problem and that these people should be removed from society forever. In other words, I think that life imprisonment should mean life imprisonment, particularly for these people. We seem to be living in a very permissive society and I believe that one of the public's concerns and anxieties is over the laxity of a penal system that allows murderers to be paroled after what seems a short time and again inflicted on the public. We as well as all the other citizens of Canada would like to believe in the parole system; that criminals should be rehabilitated and that there should be a place outside the prison walls for them. But in so far as murderers are concerned, I believe that we should apply to them severe restrictions by imprisoning them for life when they are found guilty of capital murder.
There are those who say that this is a fate worse than being committed to death. This may be true in the eyes of many. I believe, though that society as a whole wishes to preserve life, and that until fresh evidence comes forward to make a decision for us it is the best solution to what is obviously a problem in respect of which all possible solutions are not very satisfactory. I would be more happy to support this legislation if we could be assured that in committee amendments would be introduced to make a life sentence mean a life sentence. One who has committed a murder has certainly forfeited his right to continue being a citizen with the same rights and privileges as is afforded to most other people. One of the criticisms of capital punishment is that the death penalty is not applied uniformly but selectively. It is done in a way where risks are both arbitrary and discriminatory.
A recent editorial suggested that a total of 701 convicted murderers have been executed in Canada since confederation. An almost equal number, more than 600, have had their sentences commuted by the cabinet. The cabinet was exercising the Queen's prerogative, but the cabinet is a political rather than a judicial body which, by its very nature, can have no fixed criteria in such matters. I do not

see how the federal cabinet of, for that matter, any cabinet in this country could have such criteria because of their make-up.
So, Mr. Speaker, from the aforementioned figures which show that almost half of the total number of murderers in this country have had their sentences commuted by the cabinet, it is evident that sentences passed by the judiciary in carrying out justice are somewhat less than a final judgment. In other words, the judiciary, who presumably should know best and are better trained than anyone else, have had their sentences opposed in almost half of the cases where the murderer was sentenced to capital punishment.
The tide at this time seems to favour the retention of capital punishment by the public as a deterrent and as a means of stabilizing society at a time when values appear to be deteriorating and lawlessness is on the increase. I do not feel that the bill passed in 1966 has definitely proven one way or the other that capital punishment must be abolished altogether or brought back to its pre-1966 status. According to my research, it seems that there have been no hangings since December 1962, and this is significant. It seems to indicate that whatever the judiciary may say, the cabinet is very reluctant to have the death sentence carried out. But, Mr. Speaker, the public does want more assurance than it has been getting that if the death sentence is not carried out, then there must be more protection for the public within whatever means are currently available.
In committee I would hope that amendments or some indication will be made by the government that the parole system will be revamped, that murderers are not considered to be rehabilitable but that they should be removed from society for the rest of their lives. Certainly I as an individual taxpayer would be happy to pay my taxes so that these people would not be again inflicted upon society. I do not think this problem is altogether solved, because I do not think it is yet possible to ascertain just what effect the complete abolition of the death penalty would have. For this reason, unsatisfactory as it may be, I think we have to wait longer before a suitable solution may become apparent. But it seems to me that unless amendments are made to ensure that murderers are confined for life, then surely we will have to return to capital punishment as the only way that society can be protected.

subsubtopic: REINSTATEMENT OF LAW RELATING TO CAPITAL PUNISHMENT THAT EXISTED PRIOR TO DECEMBER 30, 1972
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there has been a great deal of debate in this House by many hon. members on the subject of capital punishment. Hon. members on both sides of the House have spoken both for and against the bill. Let me make it clear at the outset that I have listened to their remarks with interest and to their expressed opinions with respect. My contribution to this debate will, hopefully, be a mixture of my own personal views and the expressions of the majority of my constituents, the people of Elgin, as they have been conveyed to me by many means over past weeks and months.
I am glad to see that throughout the debate there has been consensus that the present treatment of murderers, as a substitute for capital punishment, has been far too lenient. This is a refreshing change from the position of some who have shown the most overwhelming concern for the criminal, to the point that they fail to show any

genuine concern for the innocent members of society, members of society whose lives have been jeopardized by the fact that the life of a murderer has not only been spared but that he has been permitted to walk the streets, free again, after only eight years in prison.
I understand that there have been four documented cases in this country of murderers who have been released on parole and who have killed again. I wonder whether they will be paroled after another eight years or so? People are fed up with this ridiculously lenient treatment of criminals and are becoming concerned. And deeply concerned they should be, Mr. Speaker. The average law-abiding citizen is genuinely worried about the safety of his family, the safety of his friends and himself, and is having grave misgivings about the ability of the law to offer the protection that he deserves.
Some hon. members have argued that we should ignore what appears to be a majority opinion that the death penalty should be reinstated. It is true there has been no official, scientifically planned survey to gauge the feelings of all Canadians, but judging from the response of constituents over this issue and the results of some public opinion surveys, the general opinion is that capital punishment should be retained. To completely ignore this attitude is somewhat dangerous and is a slap in the face of true democracy. I caution this House, Mr. Speaker, that we would be courting a backlash of public opinion if we were to totally ignore the arguments of many responsible constituents and the general attitude of the Canadian people.
What I particularly dislike about the present treatment of murderers is the fact that we seem to have twisted our values around. The government has permitted cold-blooded and callous murderers to walk the streets again after only eight years in prison. A thief, in many cases, can receive a longer sentence. Does this perhaps mean that the material goods stolen by a thief are worth more than the life taken by a murderer?
Surely we can all agree that murder is the worst crime; so it follows that a murderer should receive at least a harsher penalty than a person guilty of any other crime. To this extent I assume we are in general agreement. It is a little ridiculous to give a murderer about the same sentence as that given to a dangerous thief. In a sense we are equating the value of human life with that of material wealth. Fortunately, we have advanced from the time when a thief could be hung, but now we seem to have gone full tilt in the other direction and our values are just as warped as they were in earlier times. When any human life can be equated with anything other than human life, we can scarcely be surprised at the moral consequences.
The argument has been put forward by abolitionists that a civilized, compassionate society does not have the right to take a human life. I suggest that whether or not we are a civilized, compassionate society is a matter in itself for debate. Putting that aside, Mr. Speaker, I believe our society, in fact any society, has the right and indeed the responsibility to use, in the words of the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) "whatever means are necessary to protect itself from those forces that would seek to destroy it".
May 23, 1973

The ideal purpose of a society is to protect the individuals within it and to ensure their total well-being. If any members of that society are attacked from within or from without, that society is fully justified in using whatever means are necessary to defend its members. Surely we can agree that our society is justified in making war if truly endangered. This is actually a civilized and compassionate action in that it reflects a concern for the over-all wellbeing of its members. Society is justified in taking the life of a murderer who attacks it from within.
The abolitionists will argue that the death penalty is not necessary and serves no purpose in that it is not a deterrent. Some pretty convincing statistics have been presented to prove this. Most abolitionists agree that the death penalty should be retained for the murderers of policemen and prison guards. But why? Are their lives worth more than those of civilians? The answer is, of course not. Even abolitionists agree that the presence of the death penalty will deter murderers of law enforcement officers. So in fact abolitionists do agree that the presence of the death penalty does have some deterrent effect. Why should civilians not have the same right to this protection? The death penalty should apply to the premeditated murder of any citizen.
There appear to be two types of murderers. First, there are those who are mentally deranged or are suffering temporary or prolonged mental shock. The law should, and does provide for leniency in such cases. What about the brutal, callous murderer who has deliberately planned his crime and is fully aware of the consequences? How do we deal with the hired killer in organized crime who murders for money? How do we deal with the revolutionary assassin who coldly plots his crime against the very society from which he expects justice? How do we deal with such people as the bank robber who coldly informs his hostages, "I will shoot anyone in the bank, and the Supreme Court will let me get away with it. The is no death penalty, so I can shoot everyone here, then throw down the gun and walk out and they cannot put me in the electric chair"? For such people the death penalty is clearly a deterrent. They are fully aware of what they are doing and the consequence of their act.
The argument is also put forward that the death penalty is vengeance pure and simple and as such is a barbaric vestige of man's animal nature. In all honesty, is not all punishment for crime a matter of vengeance? Whatever penalty was imposed for murder, it will still be vengeance. Is not this vengeance largely the result of justifiable moral outrage by society against the viciousness of the murderer's act? Vengeance, as we call it, is actually an act of self-defence by society. A murderer kills a child, and the parent reacts by demanding his death. The murderer has in a way attacked that parent, who responds in selfdefence. In much the same way, society is a single, living unit of which its individuals are a part; an attack upon one of them is actually an attack upon society, and society has the responsibility to act defensively for the benefit of the rest of its members.
To conclude, it is the fate of a deliberate killer that we are deciding, not the barbaric means of execution used today. I believe the law should recognize all the circumstances and give the benefit of the slightest doubt. But
Capital Punishment
when the courts have referred those persons they can for psychiatric care, when they have acquitted others for lack of conclusive evidence, when social and economic conditions have been improved in order to remove the breeding grounds of crime and violence, when the penal system has been restaged to provide rehabilitative services instead of apprenticeships in crime-when all this has been done society inevitably comes face to face with the real issue in this debate.
We are dealing with the fate of a callous, brutal murderer who has planned his crime with full awareness of the consequences, has weighed the life of his victim in the balance and has valued at less than his possible gain. The death penalty would remind such a murderer who has lost any sense of the value of life that a life is in fact very dear, at least as dear as his own. What other way is there to understand the horror of taking a person's life, if not directly equating it to the life of that person's killer? In all honesty, capital punishment is an obscene thing, but I believe it is necessary to establish the value of life in our society and I will vote against the bill.

subsubtopic: REINSTATEMENT OF LAW RELATING TO CAPITAL PUNISHMENT THAT EXISTED PRIOR TO DECEMBER 30, 1972
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to take this opportunity of thanking you for allowing me to deliver my first speech in this House. Like my colleagues sitting in the House for the first time, I have been looking forward to this opportunity for some time.
The bill on capital punishment presently before us in the House is one of Canada's most explosive political and legal issues ever placed before this House. It is an issue in respect of which there are not any cut and dried answers. It is an issue which, regardless of the outcome of the vote, will never be resolved. Many of my colleagues have presented very strong and excellent arguments for and against punishment. Many members have quoted statistics to back up their stand. Yet even these statistics counterbalance each other and we are left with that nagging question as to who is right and who is wrong. Many of us in this House represent many of the religious faiths of this nation, yet even our religious leaders are divided on this issue.
Putting aside all the arguments for and against capital punishment, there still remains a basic fact which many of us, including the abolitionists, seem to have overlooked. We must all face the fact that increased permissiveness in today's society has created a climate in which respect for law and order is no longer accepted by many of its members. This being the fact, the crime rate in Canada and throughout the world has steadily increased over the past ten years, and continues to increase. This increase in crime will continue unless legislators enact stiffer laws which will make the penalty for murder and other serious offences heavier than the penalty for robbing a bank.
Every country in the world is faced with these facts, and many countries which have abolished capital punishment or placed it on a five-year trial basis are having second thoughts on the matter. England and West Germany are experiencing, as we are in North America, a new wave of thought which is leaning very strongly toward the retention of capital punishment. Our abolitionists would say to all this, "Hogwash". Nevertheless, the fact still remains

May 23, 1973
Capital Punishment
that with the increase of permissiveness in our society, our crime rate has increased and will continue to increase unless we legislate stiffer penalties for crimes committed against society.
Those of us who are retentionist are often accused of coming out of the dark ages in our ideas. Yet I wonder if man has ever, or will ever come out of the dark ages so far as his relationship with his fellow man is concerned. It seems ironical that men have walked on the face of the moon, that technology has advanced beyond man's wildest dreams, that in the field of medicine we are capable of replacing run down parts of the body with new parts and in the near future we will see a whole new generation of test tube babies, yet in spite of all man's advancements, man continues to kill his fellow man just as he did so indiscriminately in the dark ages. Have we progressed to the point that we are regressing, or has mah, with all his advancement, ever really progressed?
In our benevolent or liberal-minded attitudes today we have created a society in which the criminal elements are protected while society is left unprotected from the onslaughts of our criminals. A couple of weeks ago in the Montreal Gazette, the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) was quoted as stating that things have gone too far, and he announced an independent judicial inquiry into the recent rash of escapes from federal prisons in Quebec.
I do not doubt for a minute that the minister is sincerely concerned, but he is quite correct when he says that things have gone too far. This sort of nonsense occurred constantly during the term of office of the previous solicitor general when the government had a majority in this House. At that time the people of Canada strongly voiced their indignation, as they are doing now; but their cries of indignation went unheard. Now our Solicitor General finds himself to be a member of a minority government and neither he nor the cabinet can ignore the outcry of the Canadian people.
The Solicitor General has issued orders for stricter security measures in all federal prisons. Why was this not done before? Why was this not done during the period in office of the previous solicitor general? It is obvious to me, and I am sure to others, that the government realizes that they can no longer ignore the voice of the people and if they want to remain in power they must smarten up. Thus, stricter controls are now being initiated in all federal prisons.
The increase in crime and prison outbreaks has made a mockery of our system of justice, and all Canadians are angered and concerned and want action. I feel that this is an appropriate time to bring forth a fact that too many of us, including the present government, seem to forget once we are elected to this House, namely, that we are elected at the will of the people and for the people. I feel that it is time the present government was reminded of the fact that the people of Canada gave it a minority vote in the last election because they were not satisfied with its past performance. Unless the government smartens up and stops making excuses or appointing special inquiries, and gets down to the business of cracking down on our increase in crime and prison outbreaks, it will again soon feel the wrath of the Canadian people in the next election. Our country can no longer afford this breakdown in our

judicial system. We have seen this happen in other countries, and it has brought disastrous results. Justice can no longer continue to be mocked by our criminal elements. This is one of the many reasons why I am a retentionist.
Unlike some of my colleagues, I am mindful of what the people in my riding expect of me. I have a federal prison and a county jail in the riding of Portage, and the people who work in these places have expressed deep concern over the breakdown of penal reform in our prisons. They are also concerned about the way in which our prisoners are pampered and coddled while society is less and less protected from criminal elements. Much of the correspondence from my constituents has been in favour of the retention of capital punishment. My constituents are not pleased with the present system and they want the death penalty brought back for all murders against society, not just for the murder of prison guards and policemen. My constituents are not revenge-seeking people, but they want justice dealt out fairly. They want to feel secure in their homes. They want to know that their rights and freedoms are secure and that their lives are safe from our criminal elements.
People today are no longer fooled by political talk; to them this is no longer acceptable. They want action to curb the increase of crime in our society; and they want action, not talk, to curb prison outbreaks. We have the obligation, as their elected representatives, to provide them with such security as will protect them from our criminal elements.
Some people will argue that hanging is not humane. I agree. But can anyone in this country or in the House come up with a more humane method? Is it more humane to lock up a man for life in a prison where he is denied all the freedoms and pleasures that we enjoy and which he enjoyed before he committed his crime? We could all argue left and right on these points and not come to any agreement, but the fact still remains that we have not found a proper or workable solution in dealing with crime and penal reform.
Perhaps the old methods were not humane, but at least we had law and order and respect for law and order which we do not have today. My people want law and order and respect for law and order brought back. I am sure that this is also the wish of the people of Canada generally. Let me say in conclusion, Mr. Speaker, that the reason I shall vote for the retention of the death penalty is that I want to bring back that law and order to which the people of this country are entitled.

Some speak about the deterrent value and hinge the whole debate on that issue, yet the deterrent aspect is not the central issue. Let us look at the central issue. It appears to me that the central issue is the
May 23, 1973

responsibility of the state to render adequate protection to the individual. Accompanying this is the expectation of the individual that the state will afford security to himself, his family and his property.
Let us consider the rights of the murderer. These rights are balanced against the rights of a person who has been found guilty, after due process of the law, of wilfully and violently taking away the life of another person. Does a killer have some sacred right to life which is denied the ordinary person? Some people taking part in the controversy on capital punishment have suggested that the state does not have the right to resort to ultimate means to protect the individual citizen. I respectfully beg to disagree. If the state has the duty to protect citizens, then the state has the right to exercise the ultimate sanction in that regard. Even peacekeeping troops are given sidearms with instructions to use them if their lives are menaced. Does anyone deny the right of a government to issue those instructions?
In dealing with the harsh realities of life, societies must be prepared to face unpleasant facts, among which are murder and the homicidal urge which motivates some persons to the peril of others. Until such time as governments, by brainwashing, hypnotism or some other scientific or chemical means eliminate the urge to kill, the state must continue to retain the right to the ultimate sanction. One thing at least is certain. Capital punishment is an effective deterrent to the person to whom it is applied. He at least cannot kill again.
If the state fails to provide a degree of security sufficient to reassure individuals, then individuals will be tempted to look after their own security and we will face anarchy. This is exactly what is happening in those states where capital punishment has been suspended for a long period. Householders are arming themselves all over the United States, and that kind of violence is spreading into Canada. I think it is safe to say that our society is experiencing a wave of violence such as we have not seen for many decades. Every day newspapers carry almost unbelievable stories of shootings, murders of various kinds and other crimes too horrible to describe. Citizens feel they are without protection and that if their homes or properties are invaded they must rely on themselves for defence.
Let us look at the deterrent argument. The deterrent argument is a specious argument; it is simply a red herring. Does the threat of prison deter bank robbery? Shall we now abolish prisons? When I see what kind of people are escaping, it might be better for us to be in prison. Do fines deter speeders? Shall we abolish fines and speed limits? The threat of capital punishment deters some people and saves some lives. We know that some criminals cannot be deterred, regardless of legislation. The question is, shall they be free to kill again?
Experience shows that long-term sentences are not, and will not be carried out. Anyway, what is so humane about putting a person in jail for 25 years? Nowhere in the constitution of this nation or in the constitution of any nation does it say that a person who has wantonly and cruelly killed-that is, who has taken away someone else's
Capital Punishment
life for his own advantage-retains a God-given right to enjoy his own life. It has been held through the ages that those who wantonly take away life forfeit their own right to life. Whether one believes this or not, I submit it is difficult to make a case in favour of an inalienable right to life for confessed or convicted killers.
Most people will share the opinion that a person who wantonly kills another forfeits his own right to life. It is possible that the state, in consideration of a recommendation for mercy, may refrain from putting the death sentence into effect. No one denies that right. On the other hand, no one should deny the state the right to take away, by the most humane method possible and after due process of law, the life of a person convicted of one or more murders. The duty of this chamber is not to make the world safe for killers. It is not to underline and confirm some imaginary right to life on the part of those who have taken life. Such a right never existed.
We live in an era where violence has become a way of life, where violence is organized, where violence has been granted privileges, where violence and organized crime are apparently tax-free, as revealed in evidence in Montreal recently. The existence of professional criminals and fanatical groups dedicated to the liquidation of their imaginary enemies makes it all the more mandatory that the state must not surrender its right to defend the citizen and his family.
While I admit that polls are not infallible and are not a substitute for conscience, I am convinced in this case that the polls reflect a reality that exists in the minds and hearts of Canadians disturbed by growing violence, disturbed by the apparent inability of the state to ensure protection for themselves and their families. Surveys show that Canadians are not prepared to surrender the right to exact the ultimate penalty from confessed and convicted killers. Very few in this chamber are likely to be threatened or menaced, or have their homes or the lives of their loved ones put in danger from violent men. But in October, 1970, when fanatical groups ran riot, the situation was different. Many members of this chamber were given protection in the form of armed guards. The ordinary citizen is denied that kind of protection. He must take his chances. It is up to the state to see to it that those chances are kept at a minimum. Capital punishment is a weapon in the arsenal of national security.
The situation in the last ten years has been conducive to the utmost licence in the area of violence. The law exists but it is not applied. Either the law should be scrapped and capital punishment abolished, or the law should be applied. The present situation constitutes the worst of both worlds and is simply a wide-open invitation to kill. I strongly doubt that police and prison guards will go on meekly being targets for the violence and animosity of conscienceless individuals. Policemen are liable to start shooting back, and when they do people are going to get hurt, some of them innocent people.
A continuation of the present situation invites widespread anarchy. The present motion should be defeated and members should be given a clear choice either to retain the right of the state to undertake the ultimate sanction or abolish it. Personally, while I recognize the dedication and courage of police officers I nevertheless

May 23, 1973
Capital Punishment
feel that the life of any individual is as valuable to him and his family as that of a policeman or guard.
I do not feel that the violent removal of an individual's life by a cold-blooded killer is adequately dealt with by a few years in jail at the end of which the killer is free to kill again. The violent removal of life must be met by the power of the state to exact the ultimate penalty, otherwise we reduce murder to the rank of an ordinary misdemeanour.

subsubtopic: REINSTATEMENT OF LAW RELATING TO CAPITAL PUNISHMENT THAT EXISTED PRIOR TO DECEMBER 30, 1972
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to add my views on capital punishment. I intend to vote against the motion for continuation of the moratorium. This bill is neither an abolitionist nor a retentionist bill but is, rather, a measure of partial abolition or partial retention, whichever way one would like to look at it. The government could have introduced a bill to abolish capital punishment and we could have debated it on that basis. I think the Canadian people are ready for that question, and most of them actually think that is what we are debating.
I believe that in any society there must be law and order. Order is the prime requirement: Without it you have chaos. We ask the police to keep order and carry out our laws. They favour capital punishment; they feel it will help them to carry out their duties. I feel it is my responsibility to co-operate with them and help them, so the least I can do is to vote for capital punishment. I am not certain why they want capital punishment, and I am not sure I should question each of them about it. Governments must trust and take advice from many sources. Basically, it is simple: We ask the police to maintain law and order and they in turn ask us to retain capital punishment.
I say, let the abolitionists convince the police that capital punishment is not necessary and I will vote to abolish it. Failing that, let the abolitionists discover some other method to maintain order. I feel it is necessary to stand with the police and prison guards because I would like to encourage the best young men in Canada to become part of the police force, and I want them to feel they have the confidence and support of legislators. If we fail to do this, the police will become a law, unto themselves; they will shoot first and ask questions later. If they were about to capture a person who had killed many times, they might not be inclined to risk their lives to capture him so that he may become a guest of the state.
In this debate are we not asked to choose between life imprisonment or death for a handful of convicted murderers, on the one hand, and the morale of the police force on the other. The choice for me is a simple one. I am in sympathy with the police. I know it is not the modern thing to do, in an age when we tend to worship the misfit and apologize to him on behalf of society.
Another reason for voting against this bill, Mr. Speaker, is that I share the concern of thousands of Canadians about the rapid increase in violent crime. I know we have been quoted figures which indicate that the increase of murder has not been as rapid as the increase of lesser crimes. Is this a reason for voting for abolition? More people speed at 65 or 70 miles an hour than at 100 or 110

miles an hour, so should we lessen the penalty for speeding at 100 miles an hour?
Murder is the ultimate crime. If we lessen the penalty for murder, Canadians feel that penalties for all crimes will be lessened and that crime itself will be more acceptable to our society. This is why Canadians are urging us to retain capital punishment. They want to bring about respect for law and order in our society. They feel that if we maintain a severe penalty for the ultimate crime, the penalties for other crimes will be maintained.
The abolitionists say that it is barbaric for the state to take a man's life;-that we are committing group murder. Can the state blindly lead society,, or must it mirror society? In my opinion, in the maintenance of law and order we cannot afford to be idealistic and we can only reflect what society is. Pretending that people are good, and that if we do not hang the murderer there will be no murder, is wishful thinking. By all means let us make every effort to become more civilized. This is a challenge to our educational institutions and our churches, to our schools and universities where our society spends so much of its time and where we spend so much of our money. Let these institutions do more than mirror society. Let them lead society to greater things. But let the law and the way it is enforced reflect what society really is.
Our whole basis for law is an attempt to have the punishment fit the crime. We assume that time to everyone is precious, and to try to keep order the state says: If you break the law we will take some time away from you. This process if not new, but ancient. It is understood by everyone. We do not have laws to punish people; we have laws in an attempt to prevent crime and to protect people and property. No one desires to see the state execute anyone; the intention is that the crime be not committed in the first place. Retentionists are not blood-thirsty. We would be content if no murders were committed; then there would be no murderers to deal with.
The reason we must maintain capital punishment is that we must distinguish between crimes like making homebrew or liquor illegally, between destruction of property, between speeding on the highway or not stopping at a stop sign, between stealing of material things including money, and the taking of a human life. Without capital punishment there is no clear distinction between the taking of property and the taking of life. Surely there is a difference, but not according to the law of the last ten years. If you rob a bank, you might serve a seven-year sentence. If you rob the same bank and kill the manager, you might serve a year or two longer. Paper money and those who possess it apparently are as important as a human life. There is a difference between a human life and a material object, and our laws must indicate that difference. There must be a difference not only in time but in the kind of penalty.
The state executes many times and nothing is said. Recently a man was shot and killed as he stood in the doorway of an airplane he threatened to hijack. They managed to get him to the door, and he was holding a girl hostage with one hand. I am sure the person who gave the order to shoot was told to kill. In this case the state executed that man. He had done nothing. He had threatened to hijack the plane, but he had killed no one. The
May 23, 1973

state executed him and nothing was said. However, if he had killed the girl, had been captured and had sat in jail for months, some in our society would have heaped sympathy upon him. Perhaps 20 per cent of our society would have said, "We cannot bring back the victim; let's be easy on him."
Capital punishment is an admission that the murderer cannot be rehabilitated. This is a statement often used by those who would abolish capital punishment. I do not deny the statement, but I certainly question the ability of doctors to say for certain who will not murder again. There needs to be much more study and research done to learn about the behaviour of man before we can say who has been rehabilitated, who it is safe to return to society.
A few years ago, near where I live a man was released from a mental hospital because they said he was fit to return home. Ten days later he killed eight people. Obviously, he was a very troubled young man. In no way was he fit to return to society, but in the opinion of the doctors he was. This kind of thing happens all the time and it is the reason why Canadians are so concerned and are looking to us to restore order and bring about a society in which their families can feel safe. Mr. Speaker, it is for these reasons that I am prepared to vote against the moratorium.

subsubtopic: REINSTATEMENT OF LAW RELATING TO CAPITAL PUNISHMENT THAT EXISTED PRIOR TO DECEMBER 30, 1972
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with the knowledge that the issue of capital punishment would come before this House I have reviewed the subject extensively, taking advantage of the information provided by various parliamentary sources, reviewing numerous position papers presented by various groups, assessing press coverage and various research agencies and, above all, analysing carefully the attitude of constituents who have expressed varied opinions on the matter.
It has been my impression, and I feel it is important to emphasize this, that in the many discussions I have had with groups of individuals on the merits of capital punishment, the content of the dialogue invariably goes beyond a political discussion and each person decides the issue according to the dictates of his conscience and his judgment. It is a rare individual that will alter his opinion from reading reports, studies or statistical surveys; but it is also a rare individual that will not be aroused emotionally by acts of violence.
I would like to illustrate the latter point by referring to an article in the Chatham Daily News of January 13, 1973, which carried the headline, "Suspect picked up for the killing of Mr. Wilson." The suspect was serving a life sentence handed down in 1966 for non-capital murder of a child. The victim lived but a short distance from my home and I can assure the House that the fear experienced in our area and the criticism directed toward the ineffectiveness of our system of justice was shared by all residents, including myself.
I would like to enlarge on the matter of conscience and judgment which I referred to at the outset. The Concise Oxford Dictionary defines "conscience" as a moral sense of right and wrong, and "judgment" as a critical faculty, discernment or good sense. I wish to re-emphasize the
Capital Punishment
words "conscience" and "judgment", not to suggest that there is a similarity in meaning but, rather, to make it clear that the meaning and intent of the two words is distinctly different and in my opinion must be assessed separately before a rational union of the two can occur. If we are guided by conscience alone, a meaningful solution is not possible because the faculty to analyse all the available data has been ignored. If we are guided by judgment alone, we are then ignoring our moral values which are fundamental to our Christian way of life.
Theologians and philosophers have debated the subject of conscience for centuries. Their arguments for and against capital punishment on philosophical and religious grounds are well documented. There are those who recall Calvin's delcaration that a judge who imposes the supreme punishment is also administering devine vengeance and obeying God's orders. Others recall the words of St. Augustine in the fifth century A.D. following the murder of Christians;
We do not wish to have the sufferings of the servants of God avenged by the infliction of precisely similar injuries in the way of retaliation. Not, of course, that we object to the removal from these wicked men of the liberty to perpetrate further crimes, but our desire is rather than justice be satisfied without the taking of their lives or the maiming of their bodies in any particular; and that by such coercive measure as may be in accordance with the laws, they be drawn away from the insane frenzy to the quietness of men in their sound judgment, or compelled to give up mischievous violence and to take themselves to some useful labour.
There are those who support their views by the Judaic Christian scriptures. One position is frequently supported by Romans, chapter 13, verse 4:
For he is minister of God to thee for good. But if thou do that which is evil, be afraid; for he beareth not the sword in vain; for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil.
The other position is frequently supported by the scriptures, for example, Matthew, chapter 5, from the Sermon on the Mount;
Ye have heard that it hath been said, An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth . . . But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you.
I do not find it difficult to understand this divergence of opinion. I can appreciate the strong convictions of both groups, and I do not challenge the conscience of another individual; but I, too, have a conscience for which I am accountable to a supreme being, a conscience that has been shaped by religious and moral convictions, and in my instance, as a physician dedicated to saving lives, my conscience will not permit me to take a human life.
During my postgraduate days in Washington, D.C., I practised medicine in private and public hospitals, and at the District of Columbia General Hospital I was in close association with the Washington Penal Institution. On my return to Canada I established a medical practice and, in addition, served as a coroner. This varied experience with all elements of society, including numerous medical-legal problems, has taught me the value of human life and the tragedies accompanying death.
As I indicated previously, conscience alone without judgment cannot result in meaningful solutions. Fear exists within our society, an apprehension of excessive
4030

May 23, 1973
Capital Punishment
permissiveness is voiced by the majority of Canadians, and a genuine belief that law and order has, and is deteriorating is shared by most Canadians. I share these views and would like to take a few moments to dwell on the matter of judgment, as 1 see it, in relationship to the previous observations.
I do not intend to elaborate on the role of society and our present system of values. I shall not bore you with endless statistics and detailed studies, many of which have been adequately covered by other hon. members. But I would like to mention briefly the matters which I feel are relevant and in keeping with the thinking of most Canadians. I must concur with the comments of the hon. member for Welland (Mr. Railton) and his observations with respect to rehabilitation and parole. Although the word "rehabilitation" has been used for years, it has taken on a new meaning and new "implications in the field of psychiatry and sociology, and more particularly as it relates to penal reform.
I do not object to such studies, and indeed such should continue, but I would remind hon. members that there are adequate studies to reveal that at our present stage of development, rehabilitation in many instances is impossible. There are innumerable instances of murders committed by psychopathic personalities or schizophrenics, crimes that have been committed on impulse, without reflection and with no thought of punishment. The offender's total thought is of killing. Such a person is a threat to society and a sentence of life imprisonment should, in these circumstances, mean life in prison. The present policy of life imprisonment permits parole after ten years, and this in my judgment is neither a deterrent nor a substitute for the death penalty.
A view frequently expressed is the inherent risk that an innocent man may be put to death. I can accept this opinion and recognize that it can be substantiated by specific cases. I also recognize the great safeguards through various legal procedures to ensure the protection of the accused. What I cannot understand is the limited safeguards and ineffectiveness in the assessment of a criminal who is paroled. In my judgment, if there is the slightest risk that the criminal continues to harbour an abnormality in his psychodynamic pattern, then the public should have the assurance that such individuals are segregated from society indefinitely.
I must mention in this regard the sentence imposed by an Israeli tribunal upon the surviving Japanese terrorists who aided in the mass slaughter at the Tel Aviv airport. The tribunal maintained that life imprisonment was the worst punishment that could be imposed. Both prosecution and defence lawyers insisted that incarceration for life would be most effective in preventing a repetition of the insanity that took place in the airport customs hall.
I wish to comment briefly on the deterrent effect of the death penalty, which is the major argument presented for its retention. Despite my previous comments I have always held the view that if the death penalty was unequivocally a deterrent, I would be forced to reconsider my entire position. Extensive reviews have covered this aspect in depth and the studies agree that the present statistics provide inconclusive findings and no final consensus exists. I must make mention, however, of the study

carried out by Dr. Fattah on the deterrent effect of capital punishment with special reference to the Canadian situation. I shall not bore listeners with his detailed conclusions but simply quote from the introduction of the conclusions:
We have seen that there has been a slight increase in criminal homicide in Canada over the past eight years. Can this be attributed to the suspension of capital punishment? Now after having examined the different aspects of the problem we are able to answer this question and the answer is no!
To summarize, I feel we should abolish capital punishment; but to obtain effective reform in the Criminal Code and to offer the protection and safety our citizens demand, we must recognize that murderers are rarely amenable to rehabilitation, and major reform in the parole system is essential to ensure that life imprisonment means life imprisonment.

subsubtopic: REINSTATEMENT OF LAW RELATING TO CAPITAL PUNISHMENT THAT EXISTED PRIOR TO DECEMBER 30, 1972
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I begin these comments on a matter of such great concern for the Canadian public, especially following the diversified advertising campaing to which we have been submitted over the past few months and whose purpose was to bring the government to spend a few days debating the issue of retention or abolition of capital punishment- a debate which must be concluded by a free vote-I should like to bring to your attention the fact that at long last a member of Parliament will have the opportunity to decide freely on a very important issue of general interest. This is the part of the decision making process which is an improvement over the established custom in respect of the procedure within the political parties of our so-called democratic system. If, in the present circumstances, this practice contributes to increase in a practical way the respect for the freedom of opinion within our parliamentary institutions, we should at least have contributed to the establishment of a climate where every one could freely assume his responsibility. In fact, this is what the citizens of this country want, namely that their elected representatives decide according to the general interest of the country rather than that of a party, for the purpose of really improving the situation in all areas.
On a number of occasions, many people who are aware of the Canadian circumstances have urged that a referendum be held to give the Canadian population the opportunity to indicate its feeling on retention or abolition of capital punishment. Unfortunately, those who have been in authority for the past five years have disregarded the request for such a referendum.
In view of the present circumstances, I believe that most of my constituents share my opinion, having received a great many answers to a questionnaire; while a very limited number appear to favour the abolition of capital punishment, the majority have indicated they are in favour of its retention.
Various suggestions have been made to me concerning possible methods of execution; most of my constituents would recommend using the gas chamber, and I share this opinion.
May 23, 1973

I wish also to point out that I do not understand the reasons behind the attitude of those who claim that capital punishment can be retained for certain classes of people. I see no difference in value between the life of a father or mother, and that of a policeman or a prison guard, a manufacturer, a businessman, a poor man or a rich one. Each and all of them have a right to live.
In many fields, supervision is inadequate. It is as though the publicity media are used to adapt society to an inverted social system, for their harmful mood of irresponsibility encourages excessive laxity in publications such as newspapers and magazines, and in the broadcasting of films in which the criminals often seem like heroes, giving the impressionnable mind the most striking examples of crimes, thefts and other misconduct. After our lack of judgment in harbouring certain undesirable immigrants, we become alarmed at the consequences of our stupidities. Courts of justice sometimes become a theatre for all kinds of provocations.
Right here in the House, we have witnessed the uncovering of scandals that were hardly calculated to inculcate in citizens a respect for the established authority. Can we say now that we have used every possible means to make life pleasant for all citizens of Canada, a young country on which Providence has bestowed unlimited riches? This is the task that members of Parliament should pursue with determination, instead of talking about the abolition or retention of the death penalty. It would be much wiser, at this time, to bring about renewed hope for a better life among Canadians, by means of less materialistic and more humane legislation.
If we had a system that allowed each and every citizen to find work, or at least, a sound occupation that would be suitable to them and means of living honestly, I have good reasons to believe that the number of criminals would be reduced.
In the light of the present situation, we should try to find a middle way between excessive severity and exaggerated clemency. I feel we should try everything to rehabilitate an individual who took the wrong direction. But keeping in mind the present situation, we must necessarily adopt a position which will help reduce the number of murders. We have had the opportunity to read newspaper articles written by authorities on this issue, who recommended that capital punishment be maintained for a certain percentage of criminals. I am therefore reluctant to give a green light to the hangman.
In my opinion, capital punishment must be maintained, and that for several reasons. First of all, we must at all costs protect honest people against gangsters, offenders, thieves and mostly against murderers. It is imperative that we take right now the appropriate measures under the present circumstances. It would involve the establishment of a national indemnity fund to help dependents of murderers' victims.
I find it difficult to understand why criminals deserve so much protection against the death penalty, because nobody compels them to commit such a crime. When dealing with criminals for whom all possible means of rehabilitation have been used, with those who leave jail only to commit again the most hideous crimes, with those who have vowed to make a career for themselves in hold-
Capital Punishment
ups and looting, society has the duty to protect itself as best it can. Indulgence would then become connivance. I feel very sorry for prisoners but I do not forget the harm they are causing by their offences. May I add that, in having recourse to drastic measures, society does not take vengeance but protects itself.
